items.prompt: What's the distinction between a primary and a secondary source, per this unit?
choices: A primary source is always a printed book written by an expert, while a secondary source is always a casual website or blog post
A primary source is the original (a spec, a paper, the actual schedule); a secondary source describes or interprets a primary source — neither is inherently better, but they fail in different ways
A primary source is always more recently published and updated than any secondary source describing the same event
There's no meaningful difference at all between the two; the terms are fully interchangeable once a claim gets repeated enough
items.explanation: The distinction is about origin, not quality — a secondary source can be excellent and a primary source can be hard to parse, but knowing which one you're reading changes how much independent verification a claim from it needs.
items.reference:
Primary

The original — the schedule itself, the actual paper, the person who did it

Secondary

Describes or interprets a primary source — a forwarded screenshot, a summary

Why: the type tells you nothing about quality on its own — only how much interpretation already happened before it reached you.

items.prompt: The teacher's own posted exam schedule and a classmate's forwarded screenshot describing it are both 'sources.' Which one is primary?
choices: The forwarded screenshot, since it was taken and shared more recently than the original posting
The teacher's posted schedule — it's the original; the screenshot is a secondary description of it
Neither one — a screenshot of an official document can never count as a primary source
Whichever one has been seen and forwarded by more people in the group chat
items.explanation: Primary vs. secondary is about origin, not format or popularity. The schedule is the original fact; a screenshot describing it (even an accurate one) is one step removed, which is exactly the distinction this unit asks you to notice before trusting it.

items.prompt: Why does each layer of secondary sourcing (a source citing another secondary source, rather than the primary one) increase the risk of an error going unnoticed?
choices: It doesn't — secondary sources are equally likely to catch an error no matter how many layers removed they are from the primary source, since each one re-reads the original

Each layer is a chance for simplification or misreading, and a source that only cites another secondary source (not the primary one) isn't positioned to catch an error the earlier layer introduced, since it never compared against the original
Secondary sources only become genuinely unreliable once they're more than roughly five years old, regardless of how many times they've been re-copied
This compounding-error effect only applies to formal academic papers with citations, not to everyday claims like a rumor passed between classmates
items.explanation: This is the compounding interpretation gap — an error introduced early can propagate unchanged through later sources specifically because those later sources are citing each other, not independently checking against the primary source that could catch the error.
items.reference:
Primary→A→B→C

Why: C only ever compared itself to B — never to the primary source — so an error A introduced rides along unchecked.
items.learnMore:
The interpretation gap compounds

Each hop away from the primary source is a place where precision can quietly get lost, and nothing downstream is positioned to notice.

Primary source (ground truth)
↓ summarized, maybe imperfectly
Secondary A
↓ copied, not re-checked
Secondary B, C, ...

Common mistake

Assuming a well-written later source must have double-checked the original. Being well-written and having independently verified the primary source are unrelated.

items.prompt: Site C's write-up cites Site B, which cites Site A, which summarized the actual primary source. If Site A's summary contained a small simplification error, what happens to Site C's version?
choices: Site C automatically catches and corrects the error, since it's the one furthest from the original source
Site C almost certainly inherits the same error unchanged, because it never compared against the primary source — only against Site B
The error naturally disappears by the time it reaches Site C, the way rumors tend to self-correct
It depends entirely on how polished and well-written Site C's final write-up happens to be
items.explanation: Nothing about distance from the origin causes self-correction. If C only checked its facts against B, and B only checked against A, the error introduced at A rides along untouched, because none of the later links actually compared against the primary source.
items.reference:
Primary→A→B→C

Why: C only ever compared itself to B — never to the primary source — so an error A introduced rides along unchecked.

items.prompt: Per this unit, which is the strongest credibility signal for a claim you're evaluating?
choices: It's written in a polished, professional-looking style with no typos or awkward phrasing
Many different people and sites are independently repeating the same claim
It matches what you can independently verify against the primary source
The author of the claim has a large, visible following across several platforms
items.explanation: Matching what you can independently verify against the primary source is the actual check, not a proxy for one — polish, repetition, and audience size are all weaker signals that can be present even when a claim is wrong.
items.reference:
① Matches the primary source (strongest)
② Cites the primary source, checkably
③ Author has checkable standing
④ Many sources repeat it (weak alone)
⑤ Looks polished (weakest)

Why: the weakest signals are also the easiest to notice at a glance — which is exactly why they're most likely to substitute for real verification.

items.prompt: Why does this unit argue that a source's age should be checked against how fast its domain moves, rather than a fixed cutoff like 'anything over two years old is unreliable'?
choices: Because a source's age never actually matters once the information has already been published
Because different domains go stale at different rates — a stable-mechanism explanation stays accurate for years, while fast-moving comparative data or advisories go stale in months
Because all information of any kind becomes completely unreliable after exactly one year
Because this kind of recency check only matters for claims specifically about people
items.explanation: Age alone means nothing without knowing how fast the specific claim's domain moves — the practical question is the claim's actual staleness risk given its subject matter, not a universal age cutoff applied uniformly.
items.reference:
🐢 Slow-moving domain: age matters less vs. 🐇 Fast-moving domain: age matters more

Why: the question isn't 'how old is this' alone — it's 'how fast does this specific kind of claim go stale,' checked against the actual age.

items.prompt: Three classmates tell you the exam moved to Friday. Does that automatically make the claim three times more trustworthy than if only one had said it?
choices: Yes, always — more people independently agreeing on the same specific detail is always strictly stronger evidence than one person alone
Not necessarily — if all three are repeating the same unverified original message rather than checking independently, it's one claim repeated three times, not three independent confirmations
No — having more people repeat the exact same claim always makes it strictly less trustworthy than if only one person had said it
Only if all three classmates who repeated the claim happen to be the exact same age as each other
items.explanation: This is the corroboration trap: the number of people repeating a claim matters far less than whether they're actually independent. Three forwards of the same screenshot is one claim, not three checks.
items.reference:
👤 Senior (unnamed, unverifiable)
→ 💬 Original poster
→ 🔁 Classmate A (forwards)
→ 🔁 Classmate B (forwards)

Why: only one new claim was ever made — the two forwards don't add independent information.
items.learnMore:
The corroboration trap

Real corroboration means independent checks against the primary source, or clearly independent authors who each did their own verification — not just multiple people who happen to say the same thing.

Looks like corroboration

3 people repeating 1 unverified claim

Actually is corroboration

3 people independently checking the primary source

Common mistake

Treating a headcount of people repeating a claim as equivalent to independent evidence, without checking whether they actually verified it separately.

items.prompt: What would make three people repeating a claim genuine corroboration, rather than the corroboration trap?

If all three classmates happened to repeat the claim at roughly the same time of day
There's genuinely no way to ever tell the difference between the two kinds of agreement
items.explanation: The difference is entirely about independence of verification, not wording, timing, or headcount — three people who each separately confirmed the claim against the primary source really are stronger evidence than one.

items.prompt: Per L1, what are the three questions to ask before trusting a specific, consequential claim?
choices: How long the claim is, how recently it was posted, and who originally wrote it down

Whether it's well-written, whether it's popular, and whether it was posted recently
Whether you personally agree with it, whether you want it to be true, and whether it's convenient

② Traceable to something checkable?
③ Does this domain's age matter?

items.prompt: In L2's chain diagram (Primary → Secondary A → Secondary B → Secondary C), why is it specifically noted that 'C never touched the primary source at all'?
choices: Because C is automatically the least trustworthy link in the chain, regardless of its content
Because it means C has no way to catch an error A introduced — C only compared its writing against B, which also never checked the primary source
Because C's version of the claim doesn't actually matter to the overall argument being made
Because only a source that touches the primary source directly can ever turn out to be correct
items.explanation: The point isn't that distance itself is disqualifying — it's that C is structurally unable to catch an upstream error, because every comparison C could make (against B) never reaches back to the actual primary source.
items.reference:
Primary→A→B→C (never checked primary)

Why: distance alone isn't disqualifying — it's that nothing downstream ever compares against the actual origin.
items.learnMore:
What distance from the primary source actually costs you

Each additional hop is a place where an error could be caught — and, if no hop actually checks back against the primary source, a place where it silently isn't.

Common mistake

Assuming a longer citation chain is inherently worse. The real problem is a chain where nothing re-checks the primary source, no matter how long or short it is.

items.prompt: If Secondary source A's summary of the primary source is accurate, does it matter that B and C never checked the primary source themselves?

It's still a risk — each additional copy is a chance for a new error to be introduced during that copy, even if the original summary was accurate, and nothing downstream is positioned to catch it against the primary source
Yes, but only in the specific case where B and C each end up being read by more people than A ever was
It only starts to matter once a source somewhere in the chain is older than roughly five years old
items.explanation: Accuracy at one link doesn't guarantee accuracy downstream — B could introduce its own new error while summarizing A, and C would inherit that one too, since neither ever checks back against the primary source.

items.prompt: Per L2, why is it a problem that the weakest credibility signals (looking polished, being widely repeated) are also the easiest to spot?

Because a reader who isn't deliberately checking the stronger, harder-to-spot signals will tend to substitute the easy-but-weak ones without noticing they've done it

items.explanation: The risk is substitution: readers grab whichever signal is fastest to notice, and the fastest ones (polish, repetition) happen to be the weakest. Deliberately checking the stronger signals is the only way to avoid that default.
items.reference:
✨ Polished / widely repeated — easy to spot, weak
🔗 Cites/matches primary source — takes effort, strong

Why: the easy signal and the reliable signal aren't the same thing — defaulting to whichever is fastest to spot skips the actual check.
items.learnMore:
Easy to notice ≠ reliable

The signals that take the least effort to notice (polish, headcount) are also the ones with the weakest actual link to accuracy. That mismatch is exactly what makes them dangerous defaults.

items.prompt: The wellness blog in L3 names a journal but doesn't link the specific study. Per L3's failure modes, why is that a problem even though it technically 'cites a source'?

Why: expertise is a reasonable prior, not proof for one specific claim — even reliable people can misstate or overgeneralize a single point.

items.prompt: Per L3's last failure mode, what's the risk of applying source-verification rigor selectively based on whether a claim is convenient?
choices: There's no real risk here at all — it's simply more efficient to only verify the specific claims you're already suspicious of

It's easy to carefully trace sources when a claim contradicts what you already believe, while skipping the check when a claim conveniently confirms it — calibration should track the claim's actual stakes and reversibility, not whether verifying it would be comfortable

Selective rigor like this is only ever a real problem in formal academic contexts, not in everyday personal decisions
items.explanation: L3 explicitly warns against this bias: using verification effort as a tool to confirm pre-existing beliefs while skipping it for convenient claims undermines the entire point of calibrated source evaluation, which should track a claim's actual real-world consequences, not its comfort level.
items.reference:
😟 Inconvenient claim → gets traced carefully
😌 Convenient claim → skipped, even if equally consequential

Why: comfort is not a stakes signal — a convenient claim can be just as wrong, and just as consequential, as an inconvenient one.
items.learnMore:
Selective rigor is a bias, not a shortcut

Real calibration tracks stakes and reversibility. Using 'do I want this to be true' as the actual filter means convenient falsehoods slip through exactly when they matter most — right when you're motivated not to check.

Common mistake

Believing you're being 'appropriately skeptical' when your skepticism actually only activates for claims you already doubted.
